title: Debt and equity compared

match.reason: The closest point, bus-financing-new-business, only defines equity and debt for a new Year 11 business, while the new point compares their trade-offs in control, risk, repayments and dilution at Year 12 depth.

draft.title: Debt and equity compared
card: Money borrowed from a lender and repaid with interest. The owners keep control, and a loan is often quicker to arrange than a share issue.
Money raised by selling a share of the business. There are no repayments, but new shareholders own part of the business.
Debt adds interest payments that must be made even in a poor year. This raises the risk of the business, and a lender may take security over assets if it cannot repay.
Equity dilutes ownership, so the original owners hold a smaller share of the votes. It also dilutes profit, as profits are shared among more owners.
draft.remember: Debt costs interest and adds risk. Equity costs a share of ownership and profit.

a.q: What is a cost of raising money through equity rather than debt?
opts: The original owners hold a smaller share of the business
Fixed interest payments must be made every month
Lenders may take security over the business's assets
The owners must repay the amount raised on a set date
a.why: Selling shares brings in new owners, so the original owners hold a smaller share of control and profit. The other options describe debt, where interest, security and repayment apply. Equity has no repayments, so the last option is wrong.
a.clue: Think about who owns the business after the money comes in.

b.q: Ravi owns a bakery chain in Newcastle and wants to open a new shop. He wants to keep full control, and his profits are steady. Which choice suits him, and what is its main drawback?
opts: Borrow from a bank, but interest adds to his costs
Sell shares to investors, but his profit is shared
Borrow from a bank, but he loses some control
Sell shares to investors, but he must pay interest
b.why: Debt lets Ravi keep full control, and steady profits help him meet repayments. Its drawback is interest, which adds to costs and risk. Selling shares would give up some ownership, which he wants to avoid, and shareholders do not charge interest.
b.clue: Which source leaves ownership unchanged, and what does it charge?

a.best: The original owners hold a smaller share of the business

b.best: Borrow from a bank, but interest adds to his costs

problems.detail: Why (a) says 'so the last option is wrong', but options are shown in random order. The repayment option is not reliably last; in this order the last option is the fixed interest one. Name the option by its content instead.

'A lender may take security over assets if it cannot repay' misstates how security works: the lender takes security when the loan is made, and can claim or sell those assets if the business cannot repay. 'It' is also ambiguous (lender or business). Suggest: 'a lender may hold security over assets and can claim them if the business cannot repay.'

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The card's line about security is slightly inaccurate and ambiguous, and why (a) refers to 'the last option', which breaks when options are shuffled.
